guides.content:
# libtmux for Perl
Control tmux with explicit commands, captured graphs, and ordinary Perl arrays. Targets stable Perl 5.44.0 and Linux x86_64 LP64, including WSL. These development distributions are not published on CPAN. [Documentation](https://libtmux.org/en/perl/latest/) · [API reference](https://libtmux.org/en/perl/latest/reference/) · [Run the examples](examples/README.md) ```perl use v5.44; use LibTmux::Server; my $server = LibTmux::Server->new(socket_name => 'example'); my $snapshot = $server->snapshot; # Explicit I/O; server must already exist. my $active = $snapshot->panes ->where({ active => true, width => { -gte => 80 } }) ->grep(sub ($pane) { $pane->current_command eq 'sleep' }); for my $pane ($active->@*) { say $pane->id, ' ', $pane->window->name; } ``` | Distribution | Location | Runtime dependencies | | --- | --- | --- | | [`LibTmux`](packages/core/README.md) | [packages/core](packages/core) | Perl standard library. | | [`LibTmux-Async`](packages/async/README.md) | [packages/async](packages/async) | Versioned core, Future, IO::Async, IO::Async::Loop::Ppoll and IO::Ppoll; caller-owned Ppoll loop. | | [`LibTmux-Workspace`](packages/workspace/README.md) | [packages/workspace](packages/workspace) | Versioned core; packaged JSON loader CLI. | Start with [installation](docs/installation.md), [basic orchestration](docs/orchestration.md), and [filtering](docs/filtering.md). Read [graph identity](docs/graph.md) before working with linked windows, [query planning](docs/query-planning.md) for explicit native filters, [errors and recovery](docs/errors.md), [async execution](docs/async.md), and [workspace loading](docs/workspace.md). The [architecture decisions](docs/dev/adr/index.md) explain these contracts, their alternatives, and the upstream source models behind them. Installed API documentation uses native POD; for example `perldoc LibTmux::Server` and `perldoc LibTmux::Selection`. [Complete examples](examples/README.md) run against uniquely owned tmux sockets and assert results and cleanup. [Compatibility](docs/compatibility.md) records support for tmux 3.3a–3.8 and CI coverage of the range endpoints. Captured selections perform no tmux I/O; their methods preserve order and duplicates and return one fixed type in every calling context. Native array access remains available. MCP is excluded. Persistent control mode, streaming APIs, tmux command lists, serialized regexes, and relation pushdown are deferred. See [contributing](.github/CONTRIBUTING.md) for exact checks and tool setup, [Perl choices](.github/PERL.md) for source-backed decisions, and [branding assets](docs/branding.md) for logos and social cards.

---
title: Install from source
description: Install from source with the Perl libtmux distributions.
---

These distributions are unpublished. Use Perl 5.44.0 and install core before
workspace or optional async. Use the repository's pinned cpm author setup,
or an existing cpm installation. From the repository root:

```console
$ cpm install \
    --global \
    ./packages/core
```

```console
$ cpm install \
    --global \
    ./packages/workspace
```

```console
$ cpm install \
    --global \
    ./packages/async
```

Core and workspace need only the Perl standard library at runtime. Async adds
Future, IO::Async, IO::Async::Loop::Ppoll and IO::Ppoll. Its caller supplies a
Ppoll loop; IO::Ppoll includes an XS extension. See the
[async guide](async.md) for construction and cleanup.
Configure/test/develop requirements remain separate.
To inspect installed documentation:

```console
$ perldoc LibTmux::Server
```

The [contributor guide](../.github/CONTRIBUTING.md) documents pinned local
provisioning, archive builds, and isolated installed-consumer verification.
No PAUSE upload, tag, or release is implied by source installation.

# Examples

Run these programs from a provisioned checkout of [libtmux for Perl](../README.md).
They use Perl 5.44.0, Linux x86_64 LP64, and tmux 3.3a–3.8. The async programs
also use the dependencies in the [author setup](../.github/CONTRIBUTING.md#environment).
`Future::AsyncAwait` is needed only for `await.pl`.

## Run the examples

```console
$ mise exec -- make examples
```

The [runner](../scripts/run-examples.pl) rejects unsuccessful programs and
missing expected output. The installed-artifact CI job runs these same
programs against an isolated installation prefix. The two tmux CI cells run
them against the oldest supported and newest stable releases.

| Program | What it demonstrates | Expected result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [quickstart.pl](quickstart.pl) | Create a session, rename and split a window, add a window, and traverse a snapshot. | Two windows named `editor` and `logs`; the selected pane belongs to `editor`. |
| [selection.pl](selection.pl) | `where`, `grep`, native arrays, cardinality, compiled filters, relations, retained graphs, and native query verification. | `selection, wire, graph lifetime, quantifiers, and query: ok` |
| [workspace.pl](workspace.pl) | Plan and load a JSON workspace, then repeat it with `existing => 'skip'`. | `workspace load and repeat: ok` |
| [async.pl](async.pl) | Capture through a caller-owned Ppoll loop and wait for executor cleanup. | `async capture and cleanup: ok` |
| [await.pl](await.pl) | Use optional caller-side `async`/`await` syntax with the same core result objects. | `optional caller await syntax: ok` |
| [async-lifecycle.pl](async-lifecycle.pl) | Preserve operation failures, handle cancellation, and observe cleanup without destroying a borrowed server. | Capture, failure, and cancellation scenarios all report completed executor cleanup. |

## Server ownership

The checkout demos use the repository's fixture to create a unique socket,
ignore user tmux configuration, and verify owned process exit during cleanup.
The fixture is author tooling, not an installed package API. The runner supplies
library paths and the child-reaping scope needed by these programs.

After installing core and async, `async-lifecycle.pl` also works as a standalone
consumer program. It takes an explicit socket path for an existing server and
closes only its executor:

```console
$ perl examples/async-lifecycle.pl --help
```

Read the [async guide](../docs/async.md) before using its failure or cancellation
options. Cancellation does not prove cleanup has finished; keep driving the
loop until `close` completes successfully.

## Quote tested source

The complete programs embedded in the reader guides use `example` markers.
[The snippet check](../scripts/check-snippets.pl) compares each marked block
with its source file:

```console
$ mise exec -- make check-snippets
```

Keep the program, its expected output in the runner, and its documentation
consistent. State fixture or existing-server prerequisites next to an excerpt.
Offer a capability only after its example runs and checks the claimed result;
the [shared showcase standard](https://github.com/libtmux/docs/issues/243)
describes the evidence required by libtmux.org.

---
title: Create and observe tmux resources
description: Create and observe tmux resources with the Perl libtmux distributions.
---

Constructing `LibTmux::Server` records connection settings without I/O. Pass a
socket name or socket path; the library clears inherited `TMUX` and
`TMUX_PANE` in subprocess environments. Acquisition and mutations are explicit.

```perl
use v5.44;
use LibTmux::Server;
my $server = LibTmux::Server->new(socket_name => 'example');
my $session = $server->new_session(
    name => 'main', command => ['/bin/sleep', '120'],
);
my $window = $server->new_window(
    session => $session, name => 'api', command => ['/bin/sleep', '120'],
);
my $pane = $window->panes->one;
my $split = $server->split_pane(
    pane => $pane, horizontal => true, command => ['/bin/sleep', '120'],
);
$server->select_layout(window => $window, layout => 'even-horizontal');
my $observed = $server->snapshot;
$server->kill_session(session => $session);
```

This example creates a session and explicitly removes it. Complete executed
programs in [examples](../examples) add exception-safe owned fixture cleanup.
Literal argv does not select a shell. `shell_command` explicitly requests
shell interpretation; one-element literal commands use the core exec shim.

All mutations live on Server. Entity readers are captured and read-only;
renaming a window does not change an old Window handle. Use a new snapshot.
`capture_pane` returns bytes including tmux's final newline. `send_text`
sends literal text with optional Enter; `send_keys` accepts named tmux keys.

Use `set_option`/`get_option`/`unset_option` for explicit scopes, including
inherited reads, and environment methods for global or session values. Hooks
retain sparse indexes in native output. Buffers use stdin for binary payloads.
`cmd` is the checked literal command escape hatch; `execute` retains nonzero
command results. Ordered `batch` returns one `{result, error}` record per
independent request, not per command inside a tmux command list.

Interactive terminal ownership stays with the caller: `attach_argv` returns
argv for a caller-owned terminal; `clients` captures client data and
`detach_client` reports command acceptance. Observe client exit separately.

The complete [quickstart program](../examples/quickstart.pl) creates a session,
splits a pane, adds a window, selects a window link, and filters captured
panes. Install core first, then run it from the source checkout:

```console
$ perl examples/quickstart.pl
```

The included standard-library fixture owns its private socket and verifies
child exit. The standalone demo enables Linux x86_64 LP64 child reaping; the
borrowed Server connection API does not change the application's reaper.

title: Snapshots and linked-window identity
description: Snapshots and linked-window identity with the Perl libtmux distributions.
---

A physical window can appear at several indexes in one session and in several
sessions. `WindowLink` owns session-relative index and active state. A Pane's
`window` always returns the physical Window. Session changes use explicit links.

Snapshot `windows` and `panes` contain each physical identity once. Raw
`listings` retain contextual rows and multiplicity. Selection filters retain
their own input order and duplicates. Two occurrences of one identity still
make `one` ambiguous.

Selections may combine captures from the same server generation. Each handle
retains its own observed graph; combining them does not reconcile capture times
or create a new snapshot. Mixing server scopes or daemon generations is an
`InvalidSelection` error. Use one snapshot when a query needs one capture interval.
For example, a retained pane captured before a rename and a fresh pane with
the same resource identity can expose different window names. Each traverses
its own graph. Capture start/end metadata describes those observation intervals;
resource identity alone does not identify an observation.

IDs remain strings. Write session IDs as `'$1'` in Perl so regex captures do
not interpolate. Identity includes server, daemon generation, kind, and ID.
Captured handles prevent silent retargeting after a restart; probes and
commands remain separate observations, so they do not form a transaction.
The daemon's `socket_path` identifies the server and `pid/start_time` its
generation. Raw ID strings deliberately target current resources and convey
no historical generation protection.

The store owns scalar records and ID adjacency. Handles strongly retain that
store, which does not strongly own handles. A retained pane keeps its observed
window even when the Snapshot wrapper leaves scope. Retaining one handle can
retain the graph; `to_record` exports detached scalar data instead.
Current to-many accessors scan related records; repeated relation traversal
can repeat that work. Retained-graph memory and indexing improvements require
measurements rather than assumptions about typical tmux graph size.

Acquisition records start/end and completeness. Strict live capture rejects
missing required topology. Unloaded fields and relations throw when needed;
null and loaded-empty relations remain distinct. Accessors return independent
membership arrays. Query methods are nonmutating, while native arrays remain
mutable and every library query validates their members.

---
title: Explicit acquisition and native filters
description: Explicit acquisition and native filters with the Perl libtmux distributions.
---

`$snapshot->panes->where($criteria)` and callbacks evaluate eagerly without
I/O. `query_panes` explicitly acquires a graph and returns a PaneSelection.
`explain_panes` creates a local plan using support-floor capabilities; it does
not connect. Execution binds capabilities to the captured daemon generation.

| Policy | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `never` | Acquire and evaluate locally. |
| `auto` | Verify safe scalar native candidates; fall back to captured local results on disagreement. |
| `require` | Require complete exact lowering and native/captured agreement. |

The current implementation captures and evaluates the complete graph before
candidate verification, preserving local error behavior. It makes no I/O-saving
claim. Plans identify commands, lowered filters, residual reasons, and capability
requirements. Numeric lowering uses tmux numeric expressions. Literal operands
are escaped for the tmux grammar independently of argument-vector safety.

`auto` is the default. It costs an extra command and supervisor when lowering
is available. Select `never` when only the captured answer is needed. To inspect
the comparison, supply `on_verification => sub ($report) { ... }`. The observer
receives one detached hashref in void context; its return is ignored. It runs
inline once after a successful decision, including fallback. Exceptions
propagate unchanged unless the operation has already been cancelled;
cancellation suppresses subsequent result/error delivery.
Failed acquisition, decoding or native commands do not
invoke it and remain failures.

The report identifies `status`, `comparison`, capture generation/interval,
executed filter, residual reasons, and captured/local/native ID arrays.
`disabled` means `never`, and `local` means no safe lowering was available.
`agreed` distinguishes exact equality from partial candidate inclusion;
`disagreed` lists missing, unexpected and uncaptured IDs. `native` reports only
captured membership for the expert escape hatch. See
[`Server`'s report contract](../packages/core/lib/LibTmux/Server.pm)
and the [tested query example](../examples/selection.pl).

`require` disagreement throws `LibTmux::X::QueryMismatch`, with the report under
the `verification` key returned by `LibTmux::X::details`. The observer does not
run before that failure.
A mismatch can reflect a race, a compiler defect or a backend difference;
it does not establish which occurred. Matching observations also do not prove
an atomic capture. [ADR 0003](dev/adr/0003-query-verification-diagnostics.md)
records the diagnostic and default-policy decision.

A partial AND conjunct can prune candidates. Partial OR/NOT cannot. Relations,
null, bytes, and unsupported scalar operators remain local. Relation pushdown
and serialized regex dialects are deferred. Complete relation domains are never
pruned before `every` or `none` evaluation.

`native_filter` is an explicit expert escape hatch, exclusive with portable
criteria and pushdown policy. It selects captured root IDs and rejects new IDs
that appeared outside capture. It has native tmux semantics, not wire semantics.

---
title: Recover from failures
description: Recover from failures with the Perl libtmux distributions.
---

Errors are typed `LibTmux::X` objects with readable stringification and
applicable fields such as path, expected/received types, IDs, dispatch state,
and process result. Catch objects with stable Perl try/catch and isa:

```perl
try {
    my $only = $snapshot->panes->one({ active => true });
}
catch ($error) {
    if ($error isa LibTmux::X::NoMatch) {
        say 'No active pane in this captured selection';
    }
    else {
        die $error;
    }
}
```

`one_or_undef` handles absence and still rejects ambiguity. Acquisition errors
never become empty selections. `Unloaded` differs from known null. Complete
criteria validation runs before matching, including on empty input and in
branches that later short-circuit.

Process results distinguish stdout, stderr, exit status, signal, timeout,
spawn failure, output limit, cancellation, and dispatch uncertainty. Lifecycle
errors retain bounded partial results; unknown status remains undef.
Cancellation does not imply rollback or nonexecution. The isolated Linux
supervisor reaps its owned process group; intentionally detached daemons have
separate ownership. The current verified ABI is x86_64 LP64.

Owned supervisor and command branches close unrelated inherited descriptors,
including native descriptors without close-on-exec. The caller's handles stay
open. Only standard streams and the job's explicit protocol/cancellation pipes
survive where needed; a newly started tmux daemon cannot retain an unrelated
caller file or socket. This requires the Linux `/proc/self/fd` interface.
Descriptor enumeration/closure failure prevents dispatch and remains a typed
transport or spawn failure. Forking a host with native threads is unqualified.

Transport `timeout` bounds one command's execution loop, excluding supervisor
setup and async queue waiting. A snapshot runs several commands, each with its
own timeout; this setting is not a total snapshot deadline. Cleanup has a
separate allowance and continues after useful work expires. Async callers must
drive the borrowed loop until successful close-observer completion. Cancelling
the observer or stopping the loop does not prove that processes have exited.

`Creation` preserves a generation-scoped minimal created handle when the
command succeeded but subsequent capture failed. Inspect `created` and `cause`
before deciding cleanup. Other fields on that handle are unloaded. Workspace
uses this evidence for owned rollback and records cleanup failures separately.

---
title: Linux compatibility and qualification
description: Linux compatibility and qualification with the Perl libtmux distributions.
---

The baseline is stable Perl 5.44.0 on Linux x86_64 LP64, including WSL.
Supported tmux versions span 3.3a–3.8, including every intermediate release.
Plain tmux 3.3 is below the 3.3a support floor.
Other operating systems and Linux ABIs have not been qualified. The supervisor
refuses unsupported ABIs before dispatch instead of assuming syscall numbers.

CI and the local compatibility command use only the latest stable Perl and
two tmux releases: the oldest supported release and the newest stable release.
The current pins are [Perl 5.44.0](https://dev.perl.org/perl5/), tmux 3.3a,
and [tmux 3.8](https://github.com/tmux/tmux/releases/tag/3.8), verified on
2026-11-08. Testing the range endpoints keeps CI small; intermediate tmux
releases remain supported without separate CI cells. Older Perl releases
have no matrix cells. Update the pins when the latest stable release changes.

[The source lock](../scripts/tmux-lock.json) pins official assets,
archive hashes, source commits, and configure flags. Per-build provenance adds
compiler and executable hashes. Exact per-cell results are recorded by the
compatibility command; a missing or skipped cell remains unverified.
Earlier wider matrix runs remain historical evidence for their recorded
revisions; they do not add current completion gates.

```console
$ mise exec -- make compatibility
```

The original 3.3a run exposed tmux's invalid-layout error-pointer defect.
The public select_layout wrapper now rejects unknown/ambiguous names lacking
a custom-layout checksum prefix before dispatch. The raw command escape hatch
retains native behavior. See the contributor guide for archive consumers,
examples, units, and the network-free check/provision split.

A local test or build is not hosted CI, a CPAN publication, or a deployed site.
No unrun final-revision gate is implied by these requirements.

---
title: Load a JSON workspace
description: Load a JSON workspace with the Perl libtmux distributions.
---

The separate distribution packages the `libtmux-workspace` CLI. Validate and
plan without tmux I/O; load explicitly through public core APIs.

```json
{
  "schema": "libtmux.workspace/v1",
  "sessions": [{
    "name": "main",
    "windows": [{
      "name": "api",
      "layout": "even-horizontal",
      "panes": [
        {"command": ["/bin/sleep", "120"]},
        {"command": ["/bin/sleep", "120"], "horizontal": true}
      ]
    }]
  }]
}
```

```console
$ libtmux-workspace validate workspace.json
```

```console
$ libtmux-workspace plan workspace.json
```

```console
$ libtmux-workspace load workspace.json \
    --socket-name example \
    --existing skip
```

`--dry-run` selects a nonmutating plan. Default `existing=error` checks all
session-name conflicts before creation. `skip` preserves the entire existing
session; repeated loads create only absent sessions. This is not convergence
or reconciliation of an existing layout.

Each pane requires literal `command` argv or explicit `shell_command`.
Environment inherits workspace → session → window → pane; cwd inherits from
window unless overridden. Layout applies after splitting. Configuration is
versioned JSON; no YAML adapter or MCP consumer is selected.

On failure, inspect completed steps, failed step, created IDs, dispatch
uncertainty, and cleanup errors. Rollback targets only sessions proven created
by this invocation. Application readiness requires caller-specific assertions.
CLI exit statuses: success 0; usage/configuration 2; loading 3; conflict 4.

`LibTmux::Workspace::X::Load->report` retains each cleanup exception with its
captured target identity and attempted action. These entries replace the
earlier string-only `cleanup_errors` values. `cause` remains the original load
failure; a cleanup failure never replaces it. Catch and inspect the exception
class, dispatch evidence, and bounded native result when choosing recovery.

`report_data` returns a detached diagnostic export for JSON, including the
primary cause and cleanup error classes. Native stdout/stderr use explicit
base64 fields to preserve arbitrary octets. The CLI prints this export on
standard error; the library report keeps the original exception objects.
